known_failures.assessment: The actual 0175 asks who plans to talk; 0176 is A’s “No.” The model puts earlier 0171/0172 content under current IDs, then misreads C’s “No” as disagreement with the number thirty. Completion does not repair this grounding failure.

A says “probably not,” while the generated statement makes everyone’s non-participation certain. This exact-prompt replay has four original private-history entries; the fresh single-round call has none. One comparison cannot isolate the cause of their different errors.

The conditioned second round keeps A as the owner and adds the new end-of-week deadline. The selected passage is grounded, but the model spends substantial effort debating whether the notes represent an update or the full state.

The continuation calls old 0026 the new commitment and its final JSON repeats the old volunteering entry without the new deadline. It stops at EOS without closing the thinking block. The short 389-token output is not a successful efficiency improvement.

The control also recovers A’s end-of-week commitment, so the retained-history case does not prove a quality advantage. The “next day or two” interpretation in this same passage assumes a week boundary; the final notes also promote A’s hesitant Thursday check into a fact. Only the deadline itself is grounded.

known_failures.assessment: Actual 0516 is C’s “Yeah.” Mid-March is A’s 0517; the title/abstract sequence is A’s 0518. The conditioned and prefilled variants both shift these labels, even though the prompts contain the correct source text. Valid existing IDs are insufficient to establish grounding.

A proposes an approximate schedule; the continuation presents it as a commitment and misassigns the evidence IDs. This response closes its thinking marker, unlike the commitment continuation, but still fails content checks.
The reset control quotes these two IDs and A correctly. Its wider reasoning still speculates about exact March dates and treats acknowledgments as agreement. No full-trace quality pass is claimed.
